stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: In eighteenth-century Lyon, a large silk workshop often employed several pattern designers alongside its dozens of weavers. The ______ drawn on finely squared paper, were translated thread by thread onto the loom by assistants who read each grid square as a single crossing of warp and weft. A complex brocade could require thousands of such squares for a single repeat of its pattern.
explanation: The sketches belong to the designers, so "designers" needs an apostrophe. The passage says the workshop employed several designers, so the owner is plural and the apostrophe goes after the s: "designers'." The sketches don't own anything. They are the subject of "were translated," so "sketches" stays a plain plural with no apostrophe.

A.why: You saw that the designers own the sketches, but 's means a single designer. The passage says the workshop employed several of them.

C.why: You put the apostrophe on the wrong noun. "Designers" owns the sketches and needs it. "Sketches" owns nothing and is the subject of "were translated."

D.why: You got "designers'" right but also put an apostrophe on "sketches." That word is just a plural subject right before its verb, so it takes no apostrophe.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Hydrologist Anouk Brandt has spent a decade monitoring a high Alpine watershed fed by four glacial streams. By comparing the ______ with local rainfall records, she found that meltwater, not rain, supplies most of the watershed's flow in late summer. Her results suggest that as the glaciers shrink, the region could lose much of its dry-season water supply.
explanation: The discharge rates belong to the streams, so "streams" needs an apostrophe. The watershed is fed by four streams, so there is more than one owner and you write "streams'." The rates are what Brandt compared, and they own nothing, so "rates" stays a plain plural.

A.why: You saw that the streams own the rates, but 's means a single stream. The passage names four glacial streams.

B.why: You left the owner, "streams," without an apostrophe and gave one to "rate," which owns nothing. You also changed "rates" to the singular.

C.why: You got "streams'" right but also put an apostrophe on "rates." The rates are the object of "comparing" and don't own the phrase that follows.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Astronomer Teodora Vasquez studies irregular satellites, the small and distant moons that orbit giant planets. Of the four gas giants, Jupiter has drawn most of her attention. The ______ most of them only a few kilometers wide, follow tilted, elongated paths unlike the neat circular orbits of its large inner moons. Vasquez argues that these bodies are asteroids the planet captured early in the solar system's history.
explanation: The moons belong to the planet, so "planet" needs an apostrophe. The planet in question is Jupiter, one owner, so you write "planet's." The moons are the subject of "follow" and own nothing, so "moons" takes no apostrophe.

B.why: The mention of "four gas giants" led you to a plural owner. The sentence is about Jupiter alone, so the owner is singular.

C.why: You left the owner, "planets," without an apostrophe and gave one to "moon," which owns nothing and is the subject of "follow."

D.why: You got "planet's" right but also put an apostrophe on "moon." That noun is the plural subject of the verb "follow" and owns nothing.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Japanese woodblock prints of the Edo period usually carry only the name of the artist who designed them. Yet a team of carvers and printers stood behind every sheet. The ______ were especially demanding: working in cherry wood, they cut a separate block for each color, and a single misjudged stroke of the knife could ruin weeks of work.
explanation: The contributions belong to the carvers, so "carvers" needs an apostrophe. The passage refers to a team of carvers, more than one, so you write "carvers'." The contributions are the subject of "were" and own nothing, so "contributions" stays a plain plural.

A.why: You saw the ownership, but 's means a single carver. The passage describes a team of carvers, and the later "they" confirms there are several.

B.why: You left out the apostrophe the owner needs. Without it, "carvers contributions" is just two plurals side by side, and nothing marks that the carvers own the contributions.

D.why: You got "carvers'" right but also put an apostrophe on "contributions." That word is the plural subject right before "were" and owns nothing.

stem: Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
stimulus: Sports scientists at a Norwegian university tracked twelve competitive sprinters through a full training season. Thin pressure sensors embedded in the ______ recorded how force shifted from the forefoot toward the heel as fatigue set in during repeated runs. The researchers believe the shift, which the sprinters themselves could not feel, may be an early warning sign of overtraining.
explanation: The shoes belong to the athletes, so "athletes" needs an apostrophe. The study tracked twelve sprinters, more than one owner, so you write "athletes'." The shoes own nothing. They are the object of "in," and the verb "recorded" follows them, so "shoes" takes no apostrophe.

A.why: You saw that the athletes own the shoes, but 's means a single athlete. The study followed twelve sprinters.

C.why: You put the apostrophe on the wrong noun. "Athletes" owns the shoes and needs it. "Shoes" owns nothing and sits right before the verb "recorded."

D.why: You picked a single owner when there are twelve, and you also put an apostrophe on "shoe," which owns nothing and comes right before the verb.
